blocks.text: PART 1 — THE CAREGIVER WE PRAYED FOR

My father, Harold Ward, farmed four hundred acres of corn and soybeans outside Springfield, Missouri, for fifty years. He was a deacon at his church, a member of the county fair board, and the kind of man who still wore a tie to the bank.

My mother, June, died when he was seventy-seven. Dad was a widower for twelve years after that. He kept living in the farmhouse alone, leasing the land to a neighbor, and refusing every single suggestion that he might want to move somewhere easier.

I’m Ellen. I’m sixty-one, a retired high school librarian, and I live in Kansas City. My brother Tom is fifty-eight. He’s an engineer in St. Louis. We both visited as often as we could, but we both had jobs, children, and grandchildren of our own.

When Dad turned eighty-nine, his memory started to slip. He left burners on. He forgot his medications. Once he drove to town and could not remember how to get home. His doctor diagnosed early-stage dementia and said he should not be living alone.
Dad would not hear of a nursing home. So we found a compromise. We hired a live-in caregiver through a well-known home health agency in Springfield.

Her name was Crystal. She was thirty-eight, with long brown hair, a bright laugh, and endless patience. She cooked Dad’s favorite meals. She took him to church. She played gospel music while she cleaned and sang along. She got him walking every afternoon down the gravel lane to the mailbox and back.
Tom and I were so relieved we could have cried.
“She’s an angel,” I told my brother on the phone. “An actual answer to prayer.”
Dad seemed happier than he had been in years. He started telling jokes again. He started shaving every day.
I should have wondered why a man of eighty-nine had suddenly started shaving every day. I didn’t. I was just glad.
PART 2 — THE PHONE CALL FROM LAS VEGAS
Last spring, my phone rang on a Monday morning. It was Dad. He sounded giddy.
“Ellie, sweetheart,” he said. “I have some news.”
“Crystal and I got married,” he said. “In Las Vegas. Last weekend.”

“We got married,” he said again, laughing. “At a little chapel on the Strip. Crystal said life is short and we shouldn’t wait. I’ve never been to Las Vegas in my life! We saw the fountains at the Bellagio.”
I called Tom immediately. He was as stunned as I was.
We drove to the farm that weekend. Crystal met us at the door, beaming, with a gold band on her finger. Dad was wearing one too. He held her hand all afternoon.
Tom took me aside on the porch. “Ellen, Dad has dementia,” he said. “Can he even legally get married?”
I didn’t know. I talked to a lawyer friend, who said it was complicated. People with mild dementia can sometimes still marry. It would depend on how much he understood.
We talked about it for weeks. In the end, Tom and I made a choice we would later regret. We decided to let it be.
“He’s eighty-nine,” I said. “He’s happy. He’s lonely. Maybe it’s real. Maybe she loves him. We should be glad he has someone.”
We told ourselves we were being generous. Looking back, I think we were also being cowardly. It was easier to believe in a love story than to start a fight with our father.

That summer, I visited the farm more than usual, partly out of worry. Crystal was always warm to me. She hugged me at the door and sent me home with pie. But I noticed small things. She answered Dad’s phone when I called. She opened his mail. Once, when I asked Dad about his bank, Crystal answered for him before he could speak.
“Oh, I help him keep track of all that now,” she said with a smile. “You don’t need to worry about a thing, Ellen.”
I told myself it was normal. Caregivers help with bills. Wives help with bills. I drove home to Kansas City and did not think about it again.
PART 3 — THE WILL AND THE CLAIM
Six months later, Dad died peacefully in his sleep in the farmhouse. Crystal found him in the morning and called 911.
At the funeral, she sat in the front pew in a black dress, crying softly. Tom and I sat beside her. We held her hand. We truly believed she was grieving.

Dad’s will, written eight years earlier, before Crystal ever came into his life, left everything equally to Tom and me. The farmhouse. The four hundred acres. His savings and investments. In total, about $1.6 million.
A week after the funeral, a letter arrived from a lawyer in Springfield. He represented Crystal Ward.

The letter explained that under Missouri law, a surviving spouse has certain rights in their spouse’s estate, even if the will leaves them out. The surviving spouse can choose to take what’s called an elective share, which can amount to a large portion of the estate.

Our lawyer, a soft-spoken man named Gerald Patton, explained that depending on how it was calculated, Crystal could receive a very large share of Dad’s estate. Possibly the farmhouse itself. Possibly hundreds of thousands of dollars.
“After six months of marriage?” Tom asked, his face red.
“The law doesn’t generally care how long the marriage lasted,” Gerald said gently. “It cares whether there was a valid marriage.”
“That’s the question,” he said. “If your father lacked the capacity to marry, or if something else was wrong with the marriage, we might be able to challenge it. But those cases are hard to prove.”
I went home that night and looked at the photos from Dad’s funeral. Crystal in the front pew, crying. I could not decide if those tears were real. I still can’t.
PART 4 — THE AGENCY CALLS
Three weeks after the funeral, my cell phone rang. The caller ID said the name of the home health agency in Springfield that had placed Crystal with Dad.
A woman introduced herself as Karen Mitchell, the agency’s director.
“Mrs. Ward,” she said, “I’m so sorry about your father. We saw his obituary in the paper.”
“Thank you,” I said. “Crystal took wonderful care of him.”
“That’s actually why I’m calling,” Karen said carefully. “I’m sorry, but I need to ask you something. Was Crystal still working for your father when he passed? Still employed through our agency?”
“Well, no,” I said. “Not exactly. She was his wife.”
There was a long, long silence on the line.
Then Karen said quietly, “Ma’am, that’s the third time this year.”
I sat down on the edge of my bed. “What do you mean, the third time?”

Karen explained. Earlier that year, another elderly client the agency had placed Crystal with, an eighty-four-year-old widower in Branson, had called the agency to cancel his care. He said he did not need it anymore, because he and Crystal had gotten married. He died a few months later. His children called the agency, furious and confused.

Then, a second family called. Their father, a ninety-one-year-old retired dentist in Joplin, had been placed with Crystal briefly two years earlier. He had also married her. He was still alive, in a memory care facility now. His family had been fighting her over his assets.

“We fired her after the second family called,” Karen said. “We reported it to the state. But by then, she was already with your father under a private arrangement. She had stopped billing through us and asked him to pay her directly. We didn’t know.”

I asked Karen the question that had been sitting in my stomach like a stone. “If that dentist in Joplin is still alive, and they were married, then how could she marry my father?” > Karen said, “That’s exactly what his family has been asking.”
PART 5 — MARRIED TWICE
Gerald Patton nearly came out of his chair when I told him.
“If she was still legally married to another man when she married your father,” he said, “then her marriage to your father may be void. Not just challengeable. Void. As if it never happened.”
“Then she isn’t his surviving spouse,” Gerald said. “And she has no claim to his estate at all.”
He went to work. He requested public marriage records from Nevada and Missouri.
Crystal had married the retired dentist from Joplin, a man named Arthur Bell, in a courthouse in Arkansas two years earlier. There was no record of any divorce.
She had married the widower from Branson, a man named Walter Gaines, in Las Vegas the previous winter. Walter died four months later.
